title: Shock and Problems of Cell Proliferation
introduction: Shock is a life-threatening condition of inadequate tissue perfusion that deprives vital organs and cells of oxygen and nutrients[cite: 424]. Equally critical in medical-surgical nursing are problems of cell proliferation—cancers defined by unchecked growth, loss of apoptosis, and capacity for invasion and metastasis—where early detection, accurate staging, and risk-factor education directly improve survival[cite: 442, 444, 446, 447, 450].
learningOutcomes: 7.1 Define shock, classify its five major types using the CHANS mnemonic, and explain the pathophysiology and nursing care of cardiogenic, hypovolemic, and distributive shock[cite: 424, 428, 429, 430, 431, 432].

7.2 Differentiate the three stages along the shock continuum—compensated pre-shock, uncompensated shock, and irreversible end-organ damage—by clinical findings and nursing priorities[cite: 432, 433, 435, 436].
7.3 Compare fluid replacement options (crystalloids, colloids, and blood), vasoactive therapy, nutritional support, and respiratory support in shock management[cite: 436, 437, 438].
7.4 Summarize global cancer epidemiology, classify the four major cancer categories and Latin tissue prefixes, and distinguish benign from malignant tumours[cite: 442, 443, 446].

7.5 Explain cancer screening methods, biopsy, hyperplasia, dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, tumour grading and staging, and intrinsic versus extrinsic causes of cancer[cite: 447, 448, 449, 450, 451, 452, 453].

content.heading: Shock Classification: Cardiogenic, Hypovolemic, and Distributive Shock
content.body: Shock is a condition—not a single disease—in which tissue perfusion is inadequate to deliver oxygen and nutrients needed to support vital organs and cellular function[cite: 424]. Its five underlying types follow the mnemonic CHANS (White, Duncan & Baumle, 2013): Cardiogenic, Hypovolemic, Anaphylactic, Neurogenic, and Septic—with anaphylactic, neurogenic, and septic shock grouped together as Distributive shock[cite: 428]. Cardiogenic shock results from cardiac pump failure—most commonly myocardial infarction, or myocardial stressors (severe hypoxemia, acidosis, hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia) and myocardial defects (cardiomyopathies, valvular damage, arrhythmias)[cite: 428]. Catecholamine release causes vasoconstriction that increases cardiac workload, leading to pulmonary congestion, congestive heart failure, cool clammy skin, weak thready pulse, tachycardia, oliguria, dyspnoea, hypotension, and multiple organ failure[cite: 428, 429]. Nursing care prevents progression, monitors hemodynamic/cardiac/renal status and pulse oximetry, administers fluids cautiously to avoid pulmonary edema, and enhances comfort and line-site infection prevention[cite: 429, 430]. Hypovolemic shock—the most common form—occurs when intravascular volume drops by 15%–25% (750–1,500 mL in a 70 kg adult) from absolute losses (hemorrhage, vomiting, diarrhea) or relative losses (third spacing/capillary leakage in burns or sepsis), classified by volume loss as mild (<20%), moderate (20%–40%), or severe (>40%; Kelly, 2005)[cite: 430]. Early subtle signs include mild tachycardia and mild hypotension (systolic <80 mmHg or 40 mmHg below baseline), progressing to restlessness, cold clammy skin, arrhythmias, chest pain, and altered sensorium[cite: 431]. Under Distributive shock, Neurogenic (circulatory) shock follows autonomic nerve disruption—commonly T5 spinal cord injury, regional anaesthesia, or medullary vasomotor depression from opioids/benzodiazepines—causing massive vasodilation, blood pooling, hypotension, bradycardia, flaccid paralysis, absent reflexes, paralytic ileus, and hypothermia[cite: 431, 432]. Septic shock arises from an exaggerated systemic inflammatory response to infection with hypotension refractory to fluid resuscitation (risk factors: HIV/AIDS, ages <1 or >65, malnutrition, diabetes, leukemia, indwelling catheters), while Anaphylactic shock reflects a widespread allergic reaction[cite: 432].

content.heading: Stages of Shock Along the Continuum
content.body: Shock progresses across three clinical stages[cite: 432]. (1) Pre-shock (Compensated non-progressive shock): sympathetic catecholamines trigger a fight-or-flight response (vasoconstriction, increased heart rate and contractility) that keeps blood pressure near normal while shunting blood from skin, kidneys, and the GI tract to the heart and brain—allowing adults to compensate for up to 10% total volume loss[cite: 433]. Key signs include HR >100 bpm, respirations >20/min, cold clammy skin, mildly decreased urine output, hypoactive bowel sounds, confusion/anxiety, and respiratory alkalosis[cite: 433]. Early recognition, treating the underlying cause, fluid/medication support, and calm reassurance are critical[cite: 433, 434]. (2) Shock (Uncompensated): compensatory mechanisms fail, and the heart and kidneys show early dysfunction from ischemia and myocardial-depressing mediators[cite: 434]. Findings include systolic BP <80–90 mmHg, HR 100–150 bpm, rapid shallow respirations with crackles, mottled skin/petechiae, lethargy, metabolic acidosis (which impairs enzymatic and coagulation functions), and severely reduced urine output (<30 mL/hr or 0.5 mL/kg/hr indicating renal hypoperfusion)[cite: 433, 435]. Patients typically require ICU care—hemodynamic/ECG monitoring, ABGs, electrolytes, strict I&O, vasoactive/fluid therapy, and supportive technologies like mechanical ventilation, dialysis, or an intra-aortic balloon pump[cite: 435]. (3) End-Organ Damage (Irreversible): severe organ failure resists therapy—requiring mechanical/pharmacologic BP support to maintain Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP = [(2 x diastolic) + systolic] / 3), with erratic HR or asystole, ventilator dependence, jaundice, anuria requiring dialysis, unresponsiveness, and profound metabolic/lactic acidosis[cite: 433, 435, 436]. Because irreversibility is judged only retrospectively, nurses maintain full treatment, gentle touch, verbal explanations, and compassionate family end-of-life support[cite: 436].

content.heading: General Management Strategies in Shock
content.body: Management across all shock types combines fluid replacement, vasoactive medications, nutritional support, and respiratory support[cite: 436, 438]. Fluid resuscitation restores intravascular volume using blood (essential for hypovolemic shock due to trauma or hemorrhage), crystalloids, or colloids[cite: 436, 437, 438]. Crystalloids include 0.9% normal saline (widely available and inexpensive, but needs large volumes risking pulmonary edema), Lactated Ringer's (lactate buffers metabolic acidosis, but risks pulmonary edema in large volumes), and hypertonic saline 3%/5%/7.5% (small volume needed, but risks hypernatremia, high serum osmolality, and central pontine myelinolysis)[cite: 437]. Colloids include Albumin 5%/25% (rapidly expands plasma volume, but is expensive, donor-limited, and can cause heart failure), Dextran 40/70 (synthetic expander, but impairs platelet aggregation and is not recommended for hemorrhagic shock), and Hetastarch (synthetic, cheaper than albumin, lasts up to 36 hours, but prolongs bleeding and clotting times)[cite: 437]. Vasoactive medications stabilize hemodynamics when fluids alone cannot sustain MAP by increasing myocardial contractility, regulating heart rate, reducing myocardial resistance, and initiating vasoconstriction[cite: 437]. Early nutritional support (parenteral or enteral, always incorporating some enteral nutrition) is vital because catecholamines deplete glycogen stores within 8–10 hours, triggering skeletal muscle catabolism even in patients with ample fat stores and prolonging recovery[cite: 438]. Respiratory support delivers supplemental oxygen with continuous saturation monitoring, frequent reassurance for confused patients, and readiness for mechanical ventilation[cite: 438].

content.heading: Cancer Epidemiology, Nomenclature, and Benign vs. Malignant Tumours
content.body: Cancer is unchecked cellular proliferation progressing toward limitless expansion[cite: 442]. Globally, new cancer diagnoses rose from 12.4 million (7.6 million deaths) in 2008 to 14.1 million in 2012, with WHO projecting 26.4 million new cases and 17 million deaths by 2030—shifting heavily toward low- and middle-income countries due to population growth and aging[cite: 442]. Most cancers occur in people over age 65, with higher overall incidence in men and industrialized nations; the five most common cancers worldwide are lung, breast, colorectal, prostate, and stomach[cite: 443]. Cellular cancers fall into four broad groups: Carcinomas (most common; covering external and internal body surfaces, e.g., lung, breast, colon), Sarcomas (supporting tissues: bone, cartilage, fat, connective tissue, muscle), Lymphomas (lymph nodes and immune tissues), and Leukaemias (immature bone marrow blood cells accumulating in the bloodstream)[cite: 443]. Latin prefixes pinpoint tissue origin: adeno- (gland, e.g., breast adenocarcinoma), chondro- (cartilage), erythro- (RBC), hemangio- (blood vessels), hepato- (liver), lipo- (fat), lympho- (lymphocyte), melano- (pigment cell), myelo- (bone marrow), myo- (muscle), and osteo- (bone, e.g., osteosarcoma)[cite: 443, 444]. Cancer arises when the normal balance between cell division and apoptosis ('cell suicide' of old or damaged cells) breaks down—for instance, epidermal basal cells dividing faster than shed surface cells to form a mass (tumour or neoplasm)[cite: 444, 445]. Benign tumours grow strictly locally and cannot invade or metastasize, whereas malignant tumours ('cancer') invade neighbouring tissues, enter blood or lymph vessels, and metastasize to distant organs; metastases retain the primary tumour's name (e.g., skin melanoma spreading to the liver is metastatic melanoma, not liver cancer)[cite: 446].

content.heading: Cancer Screening, Biopsy, Cellular Changes, Grading, and Staging
content.body: Screening checks asymptomatic individuals to detect cancer early and lower mortality[cite: 447]. Cervical screening uses the Pap test (reducing cervical cancer deaths by >75% since the 1930s) alongside FDA-approved testing for the 13 high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) types[cite: 447]. Breast screening employs mammography (most beneficial as women age and enter menopause, though abnormalities require confirmatory tests)[cite: 448]. Prostate screening pairs the PSA blood test with digital rectal examination (DRE) for men aged 50+, though only 25%–30% of men biopsied for elevated PSA actually have cancer[cite: 448]. Colon screening utilizes the painless faecal occult blood test (FOBT), sigmoidoscopy (rectum and lower colon), and colonoscopy (entire colon)[cite: 448]. Definitive diagnosis requires a biopsy (surgical tissue sample, or blood sample for leukaemias) examined microscopically—supplemented by gene microarrays and proteomic profiles[cite: 448]. Microscopically, cancer cells exhibit numerous irregularly shaped dividing cells, nuclear and cellular size/shape variation, loss of specialized features and normal tissue organization, and poorly defined borders[cite: 449]. Noncancerous biopsy findings include Hyperplasia (excessive cell division with normal cell structure and orderly arrangement; reversible, e.g., hand calluses) and Dysplasia (excessive proliferation with abnormal cell structure and lost tissue arrangement; requires monitoring due to malignant potential)[cite: 449]. Severe dysplasia confined to its original site is Carcinoma in situ ('in place'), usually excised surgically before it becomes invasive[cite: 450]. Tumour Grading scores microscopic abnormality numerically—low grades (I–II) appear more normal and grow more slowly, whereas high grades (III–IV) grow rapidly, spread more often, and respond less well to therapy[cite: 450]. Tumour Staging assesses disease extent via three questions: tumour size and local invasion depth, regional lymph node spread, and distant metastasis—with lower stages carrying better survival[cite: 450].

content.heading: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Causes of Cancer
content.body: Cancer results from intrinsic factors (heredity, diet, hormones) and extrinsic factors (chemicals, radiation, viruses, bacteria)[cite: 450]. Population and migrant studies highlight environmental influence: stomach cancer is high in Japan, colon cancer in the U.S., and skin cancer in Australia, yet Japanese families migrating to the U.S. gradually adopt U.S. cancer rates[cite: 451]. Tobacco smoking is the single largest public health cancer hazard—containing over two dozen carcinogens, causing at least one in three cancer deaths, driving lung cancer, and contributing to mouth, larynx, oesophagus, stomach, pancreas, kidney, and bladder cancers (with cigars, pipes, and smokeless tobacco causing oral cancers)[cite: 451]. Low-strength ultraviolet radiation from sunlight causes skin cancer (prevented by avoiding direct sun, protective clothing, and sunscreen), whereas high-strength radiation (X-rays, radioisotopes, nuclear fallout) penetrates skin to cause internal tissue cancers[cite: 451, 452]. Carcinogens act via multistep mutations over a prolonged 'lag time'—often 20 to 30 years after starting cigarette smoking[cite: 452]. Certain cancer-causing viruses insert nucleic acids into host chromosomes: Epstein-Barr virus (Burkitt's lymphoma), HPV (cervical cancer, linked to multiple sexual partners), Hepatitis B virus (liver cancer), Human T-cell lymphotropic virus (adult T-cell leukemia), and Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV)[cite: 452, 453]. In AIDS, HIV itself does not directly cause Kaposi's sarcoma (a malignant skin blood-vessel tumour); rather, HIV-induced immunodeficiency permits KSHV infection to stimulate tumour growth[cite: 453]. Among bacteria, Helicobacter pylori (a cause of stomach ulcers) significantly raises stomach cancer risk[cite: 453].

inTextQuestions.question: In the compensated (pre-shock) stage of shock, does blood pressure typically fall immediately into abnormal limits?
inTextQuestions.answer: False; sympathetic vasoconstriction, increased heart rate, and increased contractility keep blood pressure near normal during compensated pre-shock, even while subtle signs of inadequate organ perfusion appear[cite: 433, 434].

inTextQuestions.question: Which fluid replacement should specifically be administered for hypovolemic shock caused by trauma or hemorrhage, and why is Dextran avoided?
inTextQuestions.answer: Blood should be administered for hypovolemic shock due to trauma or hemorrhage; Dextran is not recommended in hemorrhagic shock because it interferes with platelet aggregation[cite: 437, 438].

inTextQuestions.question: How does hyperplasia differ microscopically from dysplasia on a biopsy specimen?
inTextQuestions.answer: In hyperplasia, cell division is excessive but cell structure and orderly tissue arrangement remain normal and potentially reversible (e.g., a callus), whereas dysplasia shows abnormal cell structure and loss of normal tissue arrangement with potential to become malignant[cite: 449].

inTextQuestions.question: Which specific malignancy are patients with HIV/AIDS at high risk of developing, and what infectious agent directly stimulates it?
inTextQuestions.answer: Kaposi's sarcoma (a malignant tumour of skin blood vessels), which is stimulated by Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) when HIV causes immunodeficiency[cite: 453, 454].

saqs.question: Define shock, expand the CHANS mnemonic, and distinguish absolute from relative hypovolemic shock.
saqs.answer: Shock is a condition of inadequate tissue perfusion unable to deliver sufficient oxygen and nutrients to support vital organs and cellular function[cite: 424]. CHANS stands for Cardiogenic, Hypovolemic, Anaphylactic, Neurogenic, and Septic shock (the last three form distributive shock)[cite: 428]. Absolute hypovolemic shock stems from direct external fluid losses like hemorrhage, vomiting, or diarrhea, whereas relative hypovolemic shock stems from internal third-spacing/capillary leakage into interstitial spaces, as in burns or sepsis[cite: 430].

saqs.question: Compare the clinical findings across the three stages of shock (Compensated, Uncompensated, and Irreversible) for blood pressure, skin, urine output, mentation, and acid-base balance.
saqs.answer: Compensated (pre-shock): near-normal BP, cold clammy skin, mildly decreased urine output, confusion, and respiratory alkalosis[cite: 433]. Uncompensated (shock): systolic BP <80–90 mmHg, mottled skin/petechiae, severely decreased urine output (<30 mL/hr), lethargy, and metabolic acidosis[cite: 433, 435]. Irreversible (end-organ damage): BP requiring mechanical/pharmacologic support, jaundice, anuria requiring dialysis, unresponsiveness, and profound acidosis[cite: 433].

saqs.question: Explain the four general management strategies for shock, including why early nutritional support is critical.
saqs.answer: The four general strategies are fluid replacement (crystalloids, colloids, or blood to restore intravascular volume), vasoactive medications (to boost contractility, regulate heart rate, reduce resistance, and induce vasoconstriction when fluids alone cannot sustain MAP), respiratory support (oxygenation and potential ventilation), and early enteral/parenteral nutritional support[cite: 436, 437, 438]. Nutritional support is critical because early catecholamine release depletes glycogen stores within 8–10 hours, causing the body to break down lean skeletal muscle mass and markedly prolonging recovery[cite: 438].

saqs.question: Differentiate carcinomas, sarcomas, lymphomas, and leukaemias, and state the tissue of origin for the prefixes adeno-, chondro-, erythro-, hemangio-, and hepato-.
saqs.answer: Carcinomas arise from cells covering internal and external body surfaces; sarcomas arise from supporting tissues (bone, cartilage, fat, connective tissue, muscle); lymphomas arise in lymph nodes and immune tissues; and leukaemias arise from immature blood cells in bone marrow that accumulate in the bloodstream[cite: 443]. Prefixes: adeno- (gland), chondro- (cartilage), erythro- (red blood cell), hemangio- (blood vessels), and hepato- (liver)[cite: 443, 455].

saqs.question: Distinguish tumour grading from tumour staging, and list both the intrinsic and extrinsic causes of cancer along with three cancer-associated viruses.
saqs.answer: Tumour grading evaluates microscopic cellular abnormality (Grades I–II show fewer abnormalities and slower growth; Grades III–IV are highly abnormal, grow faster, and respond poorly), whereas tumour staging determines anatomical spread based on tumour size/invasion depth, regional lymph node spread, and distant metastasis[cite: 450]. Intrinsic causes include heredity, diet, and hormones; extrinsic causes include chemicals (e.g., tobacco smoke), radiation (UV and ionizing), viruses, and bacteria (Helicobacter pylori)[cite: 450, 451, 453]. Three cancer viruses are HPV (cervical cancer), Hepatitis B virus (liver cancer), and Epstein-Barr virus (Burkitt's lymphoma)[cite: 453].
